note: Real values with sources. Values marked 'tuned' are game balance, not measurements, and the game says so.

gravity.kid: Mars gravity is about 38% of Earth's. With the same take-off speed, a jump goes about 2.6 times as high; real jumping also depends on your suit and how you push off.
gravity.short: Mars has weaker gravity than Earth.

sol.kid: A sol is a solar day on Mars: about 24 Earth hours, 39 minutes and 35 seconds. This game speeds it up to five minutes for a whole day-and-night cycle.
sol.short: A Mars day lasts about 24 Earth hours and 40 minutes.

sunlight.kid: Mars is farther from the Sun, so solar panels get only about 43% of the sunlight they would on Earth.
sunlight.short: Mars gets less sunlight than Earth.

temperature.kid: The average temperature is about -59 °C. At the Viking 1 landing site it swung from -89 °C at night to -31 °C in the day.
temperature.short: Mars is cold. Your base needs heat.

air.kid: The air is 95% carbon dioxide and about 160 times thinner than Earth's. No breathing without a suit!
air.short: Mars air cannot keep us alive. Wear your suit.

distance.kid: Earth and Mars move around the Sun at different speeds, so the distance between them keeps changing.
distance.short: Earth and Mars keep moving, so their distance changes.

synodic.kid: Earth and Mars line up again about every 780 days (about 26 months).
synodic.short: Good chances to launch to Mars come about every 26 months.

surfaceDose.kid: Curiosity's RAD instrument measured an average dose equivalent of about 0.64 mSv per day during its early surface observations. Actual exposure changes with solar activity, location and shielding; this is a reference measurement, not every astronaut's dose.
surfaceDose.source: Curiosity RAD instrument - Hassler et al., Science, 2014
surfaceDose.short: Mars has radiation. A sheltered base helps.

cruiseDose.kid: During Curiosity's journey to Mars, RAD measured about 1.84 mSv per day inside the spacecraft. A future crew's exposure depends on the Sun, the trip length and spacecraft shielding.
cruiseDose.short: Spacecraft need shielding for the trip to Mars.

careerLimit.kid: NASA uses a career limit below 600 mSv effective dose from spaceflight radiation. This protects crew health; the game uses simplified radiation rules, not a medical risk calculator.
careerLimit.short: NASA limits radiation exposure to protect astronauts.

roundTrip.kid: One reference mission with 180 days each way and 500 days on Mars was estimated at roughly 1,010 mSv using RAD measurements. Other mission designs and solar conditions give different exposures; shielding is a major design challenge.
roundTrip.source: Based on Curiosity RAD measurements (Hassler et al., 2014)
roundTrip.short: Long missions need careful radiation planning.

oxygen.kid: Each astronaut breathes about 0.82 kg of oxygen every day.
oxygen.source: NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (NASA/TP-2015-218570/REV1, 2018)
oxygen.short: An astronaut uses about 0.82 kg of oxygen each day.

conjunction.kid: About every 26 months, Mars appears close to the Sun in Earth's sky. Solar plasma can disrupt radio messages, so missions pause risky commands around this period; the exact pause varies.
conjunction.short: The Sun can disrupt messages between Earth and Mars.

dustStorm.kid: In 2018 a dust storm covered the whole planet. It blocked so much sunlight that the solar-powered rover Opportunity ran out of power and never woke up.
dustStorm.source: NASA - Opportunity rover mission comes to end (2019)
dustStorm.short: Dust storms can block sunlight from solar panels.

perseverance.kid: This is NASA's Perseverance rover. It landed in Jezero Crater on 18 February 2021 to look for signs of ancient life. In this story it is 105 years old!
perseverance.short: Perseverance searches for clues to ancient life.

moxie.kid: Perseverance carried MOXIE, a machine that made real oxygen out of Martian carbon dioxide - 122 grams in total, up to 12 grams an hour. That proved astronauts could one day make their own oxygen on Mars.
moxie.short: MOXIE made oxygen from Mars air.

sls.kid: SLS (Space Launch System) is NASA's Moon rocket. It is 98 metres (322 feet) tall - taller than the Statue of Liberty - and pushes with 8.8 million pounds of thrust, 15% more than the Saturn V that took astronauts to the Moon in the 1960s.

orion.kid: Orion is the capsule the astronauts ride in. It sits on top of SLS and has a heat shield to survive coming back through Earth's air.
orion.short: Orion carries astronauts and returns them to Earth.

artemis2.kid: On 1 April 2026, SLS launched four astronauts in Orion on Artemis II - the first people to fly around the Moon in more than 50 years.
artemis2.short: Artemis II took astronauts around the Moon, without landing.

hls.kid: Orion can't land. For the landing, astronauts move into a Human Landing System (HLS) waiting near the Moon. NASA is working with SpaceX (a Moon version of Starship) and Blue Origin (Blue Moon) on landers.
hls.short: A separate lunar lander takes astronauts to the surface.

nrho.kid: A near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) is a stretched lunar orbit planned for Gateway and future operations. It supports good views of Earth and access to the lunar poles. Artemis I and II used different flight paths.
nrho.short: Gateway is planned to use a stretched orbit near the Moon.

moonToMars.kid: NASA's plan is to learn on the Moon first, then go to Mars. For Mars it is studying a 'transit habitat' with its own engines for the long trip, a lander to reach the surface, and an ascent vehicle sent ahead to bring the crew back up. The design is still being worked on.
moonToMars.short: Moon missions help us learn for future Mars journeys.

delay.kid: Radio signals travel at the speed of light, but Mars is so far away that a message takes about 3 to 22 minutes to arrive - depending on where the two planets are. No quick help from Earth!
delay.source: Worked out from NASA Mars Fact Sheet distances (54.6-401.4 million km)
delay.short: A radio message to Mars can take 3 to 22 minutes.

relay.kid: Most messages from Mars bounce off orbiters circling the planet, which pass them to NASA's giant Deep Space Network dishes on Earth. In December 2025 the MAVEN orbiter went silent, and in 2026 NASA said it could not be saved - so the other orbiters had to do more of the work.
relay.source: NASA Deep Space Network; news reports on MAVEN (2025-2026)
relay.short: Orbiters pass rover messages back to Earth.

dustPanels.kid: Dust slowly covers solar panels on Mars. The rovers Spirit and Opportunity lost power as dust built up - and got lucky when gusts of wind blew it off. Astronauts will have to clean their panels.
dustPanels.short: Dusty solar panels make less power.

blueSunset.kid: Sunsets on Mars are blue! Fine dust in the air lets blue light through near the Sun. NASA's Curiosity rover photographed one in 2015.
blueSunset.short: The glow near a Martian sunset can look blue!

dayNight.kid: A Mars solar day lasts about 24.66 Earth hours. Temperatures vary strongly by location and season: the planet's extremes range from about 20 °C to -153 °C. Those extremes are not one place's normal day and night.
dayNight.short: Keep power stored for cold nights.

marsYear.kid: A year on Mars lasts 669.6 sols (687 Earth days). Its seasons are different lengths - from about 142 to 194 sols.
marsYear.short: A Mars year lasts about 687 Earth days.

water.kid: Mars has water ice at its poles and beneath parts of the ground. Dark slope streaks are not proof of flowing water: dry sand and dust can make them too.
water.short: Mars has water ice. Dark streaks do not prove flowing water.

regolith.kid: 'Regolith' is the loose dust, soil and broken rock that covers Mars. Piling it on top of a habitat makes a thick shield against radiation - scientists have measured how much it helps.
regolith.source: Research paper on regolith shielding, JGR Planets (AGU), 2019
regolith.short: Loose surface rock and dust can help shield a base.

fission.kid: NASA is developing concepts for surface fission power. A target design would supply at least 40 kilowatts for around ten years, including at night. The game's reactor is a future technology scenario, not equipment already operating on Mars.
fission.short: A future nuclear reactor could make power at night.

marsMap.kid: NASA's Viking 1 and 2 orbiters photographed the whole of Mars in the 1970s. Scientists joined thousands of their pictures into one colour map of the planet - the one on this globe.
marsMap.source: NASA Mars Trek (Viking MDIM 2.1 colour mosaic)
marsMap.short: This globe uses a map made from Viking orbiter pictures.

edl.kid: Landing on Mars is called 'entry, descent and landing'. Perseverance went from nearly 20,000 km/h to a gentle touchdown in about seven minutes: first a heat shield hotter than 1,260 °C, then a parachute, then rocket engines.
edl.source: NASA JPL - 7 Minutes to Mars (Perseverance landing)
edl.short: Mars landing needs a heat shield and a way to slow down.

launchWindow.kid: The fuel-saving path to Mars is called a 'Hohmann transfer': half a loop around the Sun that starts at Earth's orbit and ends at Mars's orbit. It only works when Mars will be in the right place when you arrive - about every 26 months.
launchWindow.source: NASA - Basics of Space Flight, Interplanetary Trajectories
launchWindow.short: Launch timing matters: Mars must be there when you arrive.

ascent.kid: On the Artemis I launch, the two side boosters dropped off 2 minutes 12 seconds after lift-off, the escape tower came off after about 3 minutes, and the orange core stage switched off after about 8 minutes.
ascent.short: A rocket drops empty stages to lose weight.

karman.kid: The Kármán line, 100 km above Earth, is a commonly used boundary of space. Air thins gradually, so there is no solid edge to the atmosphere and other definitions exist.
karman.source: NASA Science - Earth's Atmosphere: A Multi-layered Cake
karman.short: 100 km is one common boundary of space.

orbitSpeed.kid: A spacecraft in low Earth orbit, like the International Space Station, travels at about 28,000 km/h and takes roughly 90 minutes to circle Earth. The required speed changes with orbital height.
orbitSpeed.short: Orbit means moving fast enough to keep falling around a world.

epic.kid: NASA's EPIC camera rides on the DSCOVR satellite, 1.5 million km from Earth, and photographs the whole sunlit side of our planet every day.
epic.short: EPIC photographs the sunlit side of Earth.

ingenuity.kid: Ingenuity rode to Mars under Perseverance. On 19 April 2021 it made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. It was meant to fly 5 times - it flew 72 times, until a rotor blade broke in January 2024.

mro.kid: The Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) has circled Mars since 2006. Besides taking sharp photos, it is one of the orbiters that pass messages between rovers on the ground and NASA's Deep Space Network on Earth.
mro.short: MRO photographs Mars and relays rover messages.

boosters.kid: SLS's two solid-propellant boosters supply more than 75% of its launch thrust for about two minutes. Its four core-stage RS-25 engines use liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen.
boosters.short: SLS uses solid boosters and liquid-fuel engines.

mobileLauncher.kid: SLS is put together standing up on the Mobile Launcher - a 380-foot (116 m) steel tower on a base - and then the whole thing is driven to the launch pad.
mobileLauncher.short: SLS rides to its launch pad on a huge platform.

marsSound.kid: Perseverance recorded a quiet world. Mars's thin carbon-dioxide air weakens sound much faster than Earth's air, especially high pitches. Measured sound speeds were about 240 to 250 m/s; how far a sound travels depends on its pitch and loudness.
marsSound.source: NASA JPL - What sounds captured by Perseverance reveal about Mars
marsSound.short: Sounds fade faster in Mars air, especially high pitches.

farming.kid: Astronauts on the International Space Station have grown lettuce, cabbage and even chili peppers. Growing food matters for Mars, where resupply from Earth takes months.
farming.short: Astronauts have grown and eaten plants in space.

hematite.kid: In 2004 the Opportunity rover found the ground covered in tiny grey balls nicknamed 'blueberries'. They are hematite, an iron mineral that usually forms in water - a clue that Mars was once wet. Iron like this could one day be mined to build on Mars.
hematite.short: Iron-rich Mars blueberries helped reveal ancient water.

gypsum.kid: In 2011 Opportunity found a bright vein of gypsum filling a crack in a rock. Gypsum forms when water flows through rock, and it holds water locked inside it.
gypsum.short: Gypsum is a mineral with water locked inside it.

meteorite.kid: In 2005 Opportunity found a rock the size of a basketball made of iron and nickel. It was a meteorite - the first meteorite ever found on another planet.
meteorite.short: Some rocks on Mars fell from space.

perchlorate.kid: In 2008 NASA's Phoenix lander found perchlorate salts in Mars soil. They are harmful to people, so space farms plan to grow plants in water with nutrients (hydroponics) instead of in raw Mars soil.
perchlorate.short: Raw Mars soil contains salts that can harm people.

veggie.kid: NASA's Veggie garden on the International Space Station grows plants under red, blue and green LED lights. In 2015 astronauts ate red romaine lettuce they grew in space.
veggie.short: Space gardens use coloured lights to grow plants.

samples.kid: Perseverance seals selected rock samples in tubes for possible return to Earth by a future mission. Scientists want to study them with laboratory tools too large to send to Mars.
samples.short: Perseverance stores rock samples for possible return to Earth.

cme.kid: When the Sun throws out a huge cloud of particles (a coronal mass ejection), it takes from less than a day to a few days to cross space. Space-weather forecasters watch the Sun all the time, so astronauts can be warned before it arrives.
cme.source: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center - Coronal mass ejections
cme.short: Solar eruptions can send particles toward spacecraft.

marci.kid: NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographs the whole of Mars every day with its MARCI weather camera, so scientists can watch dust storms grow and warn the rovers.
marci.short: An orbiter camera helps track Mars dust storms.

phobos.kid: Mars's moon Phobos goes round Mars so fast that, seen from the ground, it rises in the west and sets in the east - about twice every sol. The smaller moon, Deimos, looks like a bright star.
phobos.short: Phobos rises in the west on Mars!

arcadiaIce.kid: Radar on NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter found water ice less than a metre under the ground in the northern plains, such as Arcadia Planitia. That makes them a top choice for where the first astronauts could land.
arcadiaIce.source: NASA JPL - NASA's Treasure Map for Water Ice on Mars (2019)
arcadiaIce.short: Parts of the northern plains hide shallow water ice.

polarIce.kid: In 2008 NASA's Phoenix lander, far in the north of Mars, scraped the soil and found bright water ice just a few centimetres down. It slowly vanished into the thin air in the sunlight.
polarIce.short: Phoenix found ice just below the soil.

lavaTube.kid: On the giant volcano Pavonis Mons, NASA's HiRISE camera photographed a deep hole that may be the collapsed roof of a lava tube - a cave left behind by flowing lava. Metres of rock overhead could shield astronauts from radiation.
lavaTube.source: HiRISE (NASA MRO / University of Arizona) - A Giant Cave on a Giant Volcano
lavaTube.short: Some holes may open into caves left by lava.

waterRecovery.kid: On the International Space Station, machines clean used water - even sweat and urine - by distilling and filtering it. In 2023 NASA announced the station recycles 98% of its water.
waterRecovery.source: NASA - water recovery milestone on the ISS (2023)
waterRecovery.short: The space station recycles water, even from sweat.

electrolysis.kid: The space station makes oxygen for its crew by electrolysis: electricity splits water into oxygen to breathe and hydrogen. Splitting 1 litre of water gives about 0.89 kg of oxygen.
electrolysis.source: NASA - Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS)
electrolysis.short: Electricity can split water to make oxygen.

regolithDepth.kid: Scientists used radiation measured by NASA's Curiosity rover to work out how much Mars soil a base needs. Thicker soil keeps lowering the dose, but the first layers help the most - so engineers must decide how deep is deep enough.
regolithDepth.source: Research paper on regolith shielding, JGR Planets (AGU), 2019
regolithDepth.short: Shielding depth matters. Engineers test how much is enough.

gusevHematite.kid: In 2004 Spirit reached the Columbia Hills and tested a rock called Clovis. It held goethite, an iron mineral that only forms with water. Rocks in the hills also held hematite. Iron like this could one day help build on Mars.
gusevHematite.short: Spirit found water-made iron minerals in the hills.

sulfateSalt.kid: In 2005 Spirit's wheels dug up bright soil on Husband Hill, named Paso Robles. It was the saltiest soil found on Mars so far, mostly an iron sulfate salt with water locked inside. Spirit found more at Arad and Tyrone. This soil is soft, so rover wheels slip in it.
sulfateSalt.source: NASA: Bright soil near McCool, salty deja vu
sulfateSalt.short: Salty soil in Gusev holds water inside it.

gusevMeteorite.kid: In 2006 Spirit spotted two smooth, shiny rocks and named them Allan Hills and Zhong Shan. They looked like iron meteorites: iron and nickel that fell from space. Meteorites are easiest to spot on smooth, flat ground.
gusevMeteorite.short: Spirit spotted two likely iron meteorites.

silica.kid: Next to Home Plate, Spirit's dragging wheel dug up soil that was about 90 percent silica. Silica is what glass is made from. On Earth, soil like this forms at hot springs and steam vents.
silica.short: Silica makes glass, and hints at hot water.

carbonate.kid: Spirit studied a rock outcrop called Comanche in 2005. Years later, scientists worked out that it held 16 to 34 percent carbonate. Carbonate forms in water that is not acid, which is kinder to life.
carbonate.short: Comanche's carbonate points to gentle, neutral water.

tuned.note: These are game balance numbers so a whole mission fits into minutes of play. They are NOT measurements.
tuned.solSeconds: A full day/night cycle takes 5 real minutes at normal speed. One real Martian sol is about 24 Earth hours 39 minutes (24.66 hours).
tuned.solarStormDose: Solar storm radiation is made stronger than reality so you can see shielding matter within one game
tuned.kWhPerPanel: Each solar panel makes 6 kWh per clear sol in the game
